clue.text: Books from dump missing covers and devoured by rodents

indicators.note: what is devoured ends up inside the eater, so one piece goes within the other

parts.note: voles are small rodents

indicators.note: covers are the outside layers, so losing them leaves only the inner letters of the word

parts.note: the word with its first and last letters stripped

explanation.surface: Old books from a rubbish tip, their covers gone, have been gnawed by rats and mice.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Covers' sounds like book covers in this scene, but it means the outer letters of 'dump'.
explanation.definitionFit: A volume is a single book, especially one of a set, so plural volumes are books.

clue.text: Victors guarding island in an indolent manner, clearly

indicators.note: a guard surrounds what it protects, so the letters close round another piece

parts.note: V is the abbreviation for victor, and two victors give two Vs
I is the standard abbreviation for island
doing something idly is doing it lazily

explanation.surface: Winners protect an island, lazily, and plainly so.
explanation.walkthrough: The plural 'Victors' is the clue to use V twice, with the island letter between them, before IDLY follows.
explanation.definitionFit: Something described vividly is presented in sharp, distinct, easily seen terms, so the adverbs are close synonyms.

clue.text: Write rules and pin one above blackboard

indicators.note: in a down entry one piece sitting over another means it comes first in the reading order

parts.note: pins is slang for legs, so a pin is a leg
the Roman numeral for one
a slate was the schoolroom writing board

explanation.surface: A teacher writes up the class rules and pins a notice above the blackboard.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pin' looks like a verb for fixing a notice, but it is a noun: pins are informal legs.
explanation.definitionFit: To legislate is to make laws, and drafting rules for a country or body is exactly that activity.

clue.text: Institute providing support for fellow with a mental condition

indicators.note: in a down entry a support sits underneath, so this piece is placed after the one it holds up

parts.note: a fellow is a man
I is an abbreviation for institute
taken as written

explanation.surface: A care institution supports a man suffering from a psychiatric illness.
explanation.walkthrough: Although Institute is the first word, it is placed beneath the fellow, so the letters read MAN then I then A.
explanation.definitionFit: Mania is a psychiatric state of abnormally elevated mood and energy, a recognised disorder of the mind.

clue.text: Gladiator fights nursing a cut, amazingly

indicators.note: to nurse something is to hold it close, so one piece cradles the other

parts.note: to spar is to fight, as boxers do

indicators.note: something amazing is astonishing and out of the ordinary, so these letters come out in an unexpected order

parts.note: taken as written, to be rearranged

explanation.surface: A gladiator keeps on fighting despite carrying a wound, astonishingly.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fights' is a verb in the surface but supplies a word from boxing practice, which opens up near its end to take the jumbled letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Spartacus was the Thracian slave trained in the arena who led a famous revolt against Rome.

clue.text: Arab revolutionary claims it's difficult to get job

indicators.note: a revolution is a turning round, so the word is turned back to front
to claim is to take hold of something, so one piece takes in another

parts.note: taken as written, to be turned round

indicators.note: a difficult thing is awkward or troublesome, so these letters are jumbled

parts.note: taken as written, to be rearranged

explanation.surface: A rebel in the Middle East complains that finding work is hard.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Arab revolutionary' reads as a political rebel, but it is the word itself spun round to BARA, which then holds IST.
explanation.definitionFit: Making espresso drinks in a coffee shop is an occupation, so the job title works as a crossword-style definition.

clue.text: Burglars initially lie about fire

indicators.note: initially means at the start, so only the opening letter of the word is used

parts.note: the first letter of the word
to lie about is to lounge around idly

explanation.surface: Burglars deny the fire, lying about how it started.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Lie about' suggests telling untruths, but it means lounging, which is LAZE.
explanation.definitionFit: A blaze is a large, fiercely burning fire, so the noun is a direct synonym.

clue.text: Anger about commotion outside hotel's American bar

indicators.note: about means around, so the outer word wraps round the rest

parts.note: to rouse someone is to stir them to anger

indicators.note: being outside something means surrounding it, so this piece encloses another

parts.note: ado is fuss or commotion
H is hotel in the phonetic alphabet

explanation.surface: Someone is furious about the uproar outside a hotel's American-style bar.
explanation.walkthrough: There are two layers of wrapping: the commotion goes round the hotel first, and that whole unit then sits inside the verb for anger.
explanation.definitionFit: In the United States a roadhouse is a tavern or inn on a highway serving drinks, meals and often music.

clue.text: Some knit a scarf, having spun material

indicators.note: spinning turns a thing round, so the letters run backwards
some means part of, so the answer is a portion of the words that follow

parts.note: the run of letters across the word boundaries, before turning

explanation.surface: Some people knit a scarf after spinning their own yarn.
explanation.walkthrough: The letters NITAS sit inside 'knit a scarf'; read backwards they give SATIN.
explanation.definitionFit: Satin is a smooth, glossy woven fabric, so it is an example of a material.

clue.text: Prune tips of azalea bush on hilltop

indicators.note: in a down entry one piece placed on another comes above it, so it is read first
the tip of a word is its first letter, so only the leading letters are kept

parts.note: the first letter of each of the two words
a ridge is the long narrow crest of a hill

explanation.surface: A gardener trims back the ends of an azalea growing on top of a hill.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Prune' looks like gardening alongside the azalea, but it is the definition, used in the sense of cutting text.
explanation.definitionFit: To abridge a text is to shorten it by cutting, just as pruning cuts back excess growth.

clue.text: One following strict diet, say, squeezed into vehicle

indicators.note: something squeezed into a space ends up inside it

parts.note: a van is a vehicle
e.g. means for example, as 'say' does

explanation.surface: A dieter, perhaps, is crammed into a car.
explanation.walkthrough: The comma splits off 'say', which is not a verb of speaking but the abbreviation for 'for example'.
explanation.definitionFit: A vegan eats no animal products at all, a rigorous regime compared with ordinary eating.

clue.text: A dog tears around rock

parts.note: taken as written

indicators.note: turning things around muddles their order, so these letters are rearranged

parts.note: a lab is a Labrador retriever
taken as written, to be rearranged

explanation.surface: A dog races about over a boulder.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tears' reads as a verb of rushing, but it is simply the letters to be mixed up.
explanation.definitionFit: Alabaster is a fine-grained mineral, a form of gypsum carved for ornaments, so it is a kind of stone.

clue.text: Demolish theatre in very poor quarter

indicators.note: one thing being in another means it sits inside it

parts.note: dismal means dreadful or of very low quality
NT is the National Theatre in London
east is one of the four compass points, or quarters

explanation.surface: Pull down the theatre in a deprived district of town.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Very poor quarter' looks like a slum, but it splits into DISMAL and a compass point.
explanation.definitionFit: To dismantle is to take something apart piece by piece, close to knocking it down.

clue.text: Refined sweetheart taking year off before degree

indicators.note: before means in front of, so this piece comes first
taking something away removes it, and with the word that follows it signals a dropped letter
taking something off removes it, so a letter is dropped

parts.note: honey is a term of endearment
Y is the abbreviation for year
D is the abbreviation for degree

explanation.surface: A cultured lover takes a gap year before going to university.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Taking year off' evokes a gap year, but it means removing Y from HONEY.
explanation.definitionFit: Honed skills have been sharpened and perfected through practice, which is what refined means here.

clue.text: Playwright scoffs behind enemy's back

indicators.note: behind means following, so this piece comes after the other
the back of a word is its final letter

parts.note: the last letter of the word
to scoff food is to eat it greedily

explanation.surface: A dramatist mocks a rival behind their back.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Scoffs' suggests mocking, but it is the British slang sense of gobbling food.
explanation.definitionFit: W. B. Yeats, the Irish poet, also wrote many plays and co-founded Dublin's Abbey Theatre.

clue.text: Friends rolled joint in perverse kind of comedy

indicators.note: rolling something over turns it round, so the letters run backwards

parts.note: pals are friends

indicators.note: one thing being in another means it sits inside it

parts.note: sick humour is perverse or morbid
a T is a T-shaped pipe joint

explanation.surface: Friends roll a spliff while watching some twisted comedy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rolled joint' suggests a cannabis cigarette, but 'rolled' turns the friends round and 'joint' is the letter T, from the T-shaped pipe fitting.
explanation.definitionFit: Slapstick is boisterous physical comedy built on pratfalls and knockabout, one recognised genre of humour.

clue.text: Motor originally bought by relative is a gem

parts.note: a motor is a car

indicators.note: originally means at the start, so only the opening letter of the word is used

parts.note: the first letter of the word
an uncle is a relative

explanation.surface: A car first bought by a family member is a real treasure.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Motor' is everyday British slang for a car.
explanation.definitionFit: A carbuncle is a red garnet cut into a rounded dome shape, a precious stone.

clue.text: Making a comeback, ruler takes second Sumerian city

indicators.note: taking something in means holding it inside

parts.note: a regent rules in place of a monarch
S is the abbreviation for second
Ur was an ancient city of Sumer in Mesopotamia

explanation.surface: A returning king captures a second ancient Mesopotamian city.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Ruler' is not a measuring stick but one who reigns in a monarch's place; Ur is the ancient city in what is now Iraq.
explanation.definitionFit: Resurgent describes something rising again after a decline, the adjective for staging a revival.

clue.text: Euphoric old hack is drunk in supermarket

indicators.note: one thing being in another means it sits inside it
someone drunk is unsteady and muddled, so these letters reel into a new order

parts.note: taken as written, to be rearranged
the Co-op is a British chain of supermarkets
O is the abbreviation for old

explanation.surface: A veteran journalist, merry on drink, is found in the supermarket.
explanation.walkthrough: The Co-op is a British supermarket chain; the jumbled O and HACK sit inside it.
explanation.definitionFit: Cock-a-hoop is an old idiom for being jubilant and crowing with delight, so it means elated.

clue.text: Cracks about clergyman meeting clowns

parts.note: c. is the abbreviation for circa, about
Rev is short for reverend
asses are fools or clowns

explanation.surface: Jokes are told about a vicar meeting a troupe of clowns.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cracks' looks like jokes, and 'about' like a container signal, but it simply gives C.
explanation.definitionFit: A crevasse is a deep crack or fissure, especially in a glacier, so the plurals match.

clue.text: Queen enters church toilet with extremely unkempt hairstyle

indicators.note: whatever enters a place ends up inside it

parts.note: CE is the Church of England
WC is water closet

indicators.note: the extremes of a word are its two end letters

parts.note: the first and last letters of the word
R for Regina, Latin for queen

explanation.surface: The Queen walks into a church lavatory with very messy hair.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Extremely' looks like 'very', but it keeps just the ends of 'unkempt'.
explanation.definitionFit: A crew cut is a very short, bristly haircut, one style of cutting hair.

clue.text: Top 40 on the radio

indicators.note: radio is heard, not read, so the answer is what a listener would hear

parts.note: XL is 40 in Roman numerals

explanation.surface: A countdown of the forty best-selling records, broadcast on air.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Top 40' reads as the chart show; split it, and 40 is XL, which said out loud gives the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: To top a rival is to surpass or outdo them, and to excel is to be better than others.

clue.text: Most sumptuous female consumed by desire

indicators.note: what is consumed goes inside the consumer

parts.note: lust is strong desire
she is the female pronoun

explanation.surface: The most luxurious woman is overcome by longing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Consumed by desire' reads as an idiom for passion, but it literally puts the female pronoun inside the word for desire.
explanation.definitionFit: Lush means rich and luxurious, so the superlative is the most opulent or lavish.

clue.text: English musketeer lacks a moral code

parts.note: E is the abbreviation for English

indicators.note: lacking something means being without it, so a letter is dropped

parts.note: Athos is one of Dumas's Three Musketeers
taken as written, the letter that goes

explanation.surface: An English swordsman has no principles.
explanation.walkthrough: The musketeer is Athos, from Dumas; removing 'a' leaves THOS after E.
explanation.definitionFit: An ethos is the guiding beliefs and values of a person or group, its set of principles.

clue.text: Government department defends article on international capital

indicators.note: in a down entry a piece placed on another sits above it, so it comes first
a defender stands round what it protects, so one piece encloses another

parts.note: HO is the Home Office, a UK government department
an is the indefinite article
I is the abbreviation for international

explanation.surface: A ministry defends a newspaper article on global finance.
explanation.walkthrough: 'International capital' looks like money moving across borders, but 'capital' alone is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Hanoi is the capital city of Vietnam.

clue.text: Predecessors hog markets for Spooner

indicators.note: the Reverend Spooner swapped the opening sounds of words, so the initial sounds trade places

parts.note: a hog is a boar; its opening B sound is traded for the F of the next word
markets are fairs; the opening F sound is traded for the B of the previous word

explanation.surface: Our ancestors monopolised the markets, says the Reverend Spooner.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hog' looks like a verb meaning to monopolise, but it is the noun boar; BOAR FAIRS with the first sounds swapped is FORE BEARS.
explanation.definitionFit: Forebears are ancestors, the people who came before us in a family line.

clue.text: Swift measures blocked by Left

indicators.note: something blocked has an obstacle stuck in its middle

parts.note: feet are units of length
L is the abbreviation for left

explanation.surface: Quick policies are obstructed by left-wing politicians.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Swift' looks like the satirist Jonathan Swift, but it is the adjective; L goes inside FEET.
explanation.definitionFit: Fleet as an adjective means fast or nimble, as in fleet of foot.

clue.text: Make cross hand gesture

parts.note: surface reading: an angry person makes a rude sign with their hand
setter's reading: a priest traces the sign of the cross with a raised hand

explanation.walkthrough: 'Cross' reads as angry, as if describing a rude gesture, but it is the Christian cross traced in the air.
explanation.definitionFit: A priest gives a blessing by marking the sign of the cross with the hand over someone.

clue.text: Enticed unfit to embrace exercise bug

indicators.note: an embrace wraps round someone, so one piece encloses another
something unfit is in poor shape, so these letters are reshaped

parts.note: taken as written, to be rearranged
PE is physical education

explanation.surface: Someone out of shape was tempted into a workout by the fitness bug.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Exercise bug' suggests enthusiasm for fitness, but 'bug' alone is the definition, in the loose sense of a creepy-crawly.
explanation.definitionFit: Bug is used informally for any small creepy-crawly, and a centipede is a many-legged arthropod.

clue.text: Call up First Lady about Oklahoma

indicators.note: about means around, so the outer word wraps round the rest

parts.note: Eve was the first woman in the Bible
OK is the postal abbreviation for Oklahoma

explanation.surface: Phone the President's wife concerning Oklahoma.
explanation.walkthrough: 'First Lady' suggests the US President's wife, but it is the first woman, Eve.
explanation.definitionFit: To evoke a memory is to summon or bring it to mind, just as calling up a memory does.

clue.text: Itinerant almost steals King Tut's head ornament

indicators.note: a thief takes the stolen thing in, so one piece goes inside another
almost means not quite all, so the last letter is cut

parts.note: a tinker was a travelling mender of pots
R for Rex, Latin for king

indicators.note: the head of a word is its first letter

parts.note: the first letter of the word

explanation.surface: A wandering thief nearly makes off with the pharaoh Tutankhamun's headdress.
explanation.walkthrough: TINKER loses its last letter, takes R after its T, and the head of Tut follows.
explanation.definitionFit: A trinket is a small cheap ornament or piece of jewellery of little value.

clue.text: Alcoholic has fling with Mary Jane

parts.note: to fling is to toss
Mary Jane and pot are both slang for marijuana

explanation.surface: A heavy drinker has an affair with a woman called Mary Jane.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fling' reads as an affair, and Mary Jane as a woman, but they are a verb and drug slang.
explanation.definitionFit: Tosspot is an old word for a habitual drunkard, one who tosses back pots of ale.
